title: Is Watching Videos at 2x Speed a Bad Idea?
author: Veronique Greenwood
body:
In You Can See Everything, the documentary about Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes and her husband Billy Evans, Evans is often seen busily watching videos on 2x speed. He’s not the only one; many people, especially younger ones, are playing video and audio content at faster speeds to get through the material more quickly. In 2022, a YouGov poll found that 11% of respondents reported having watched sped-up content, and in a 2024 paper, 84% of surveyed university students reported doing it with taped lectures. We asked researchers whether this is actually an effective way to learn.

Does speeding content up make it harder to retain?

With training, the human ear can handle some pretty impressive speeds, says Marcus Pearce, a cognitive scientist at Queen Mary University of London. “The average rate of speech is around 150-200 words per minute,” he says. “But we can understand speech up to about double that.” He describes a blind colleague who used screen reading software that read his emails aloud at about 400 to 500 words per minute, “which sounds like gobbledygook unless you're used to it,” he says. “There definitely is an effect of training. You can train your brain to do it.”

A 2025 metanalysis of 24 studies looked at whether speeding up video lectures made people perform worse on assessments afterwards, and the authors concluded that up to 1.5x, there wasn’t much of a negative effect on people’s scores. Above 2x, the negative effect grew larger.

“At two times playback speed, then memory performance is quite significantly impaired,” says Pearce, who wasn’t involved in the paper but wrote an analysis of it. “So if you go up to two and a half times, then on average it would be about a 17%” decline in scores.

Pearce thinks this may have to do with working memory, the system we use to take in information, compare it to what we already know, and stash it in long-term memory. “Working memory importantly has a limited capacity,” he says. “So it can get overloaded if too much information comes in at one time.”

Is there a way to make speeding through content more efficient?

One way to help your brain retain information is to include video, slides with text, or images in the material you’re speeding through—in other words, to not just rely on sound for the information, says Ashley Chen, a cognitive psychologist at University of California, Los Angeles, who has authored articles on speed-watching and speed-listening.

In one set of studies, “we saw that the audiovisual group actually significantly outperformed the audio-only group on a later test,” she says. “And interestingly, there were no differences in performance between the 1x- and 2x-speed audiovisual groups. So this suggests to us that pairing narration with some sort of visual component to learning can help mitigate the negative effects we see with accelerated playback speeds.”

Taking notes while watching helps too, Chen and colleagues have found. People who took notes while watching at 2x speed performed better later on a quiz of the information than people who watched at 1x speed and took no notes.

Will watching at 2x-speed negatively affect the brain?

“The long-term effects I think are not really known,” says Pearce. “There's not really been much evidence scientifically.”

While it’s outside the scope of her memory research, Chen says she understands why people might be worried. “On one hand, I think faster playback speed can potentially limit mind wandering, maybe encourage more sustained engagement of information,” she says, pointing to the work of her coauthor, Dillon Murphy, who has studied lecture speed and mind-wandering and found lower rates when watching videos faster.

On the other hand, watching or listening at high speed might be more mentally taxing than at a normal speed, and it may affect people’s ability to sustain their attention when doing slower activities, she says. “As it stands, we don't yet have sufficient evidence to draw very strong conclusions about this.

“But I do think it is a very interesting question,” she says, “especially as more and more individuals start accelerating playback speed, and maybe starting at an even younger age than our current generation of students.”
